kp.k: Susskind predicts unusually rapid transformation of legal services
kp.d: The publisher's description presents Susskind's forecast of more legal change over the coming two decades than over the preceding two centuries. The third edition focuses on the 2020s. These are prospective claims conveyed by a book listing, not empirical findings or arguments reproduced from the full book.
qs: Predicts more change in law in the coming two decades than we have seen in the past two centuries
The third edition focuses on the law and lawyers in the 2020s.

kp.k: AI accompanies broader market and service-delivery restructuring
kp.d: The description attributes to Susskind a future combining AI-based global legal businesses, disruptive technologies, liberalized markets, commoditization and alternative sourcing. This frames AI as part of broader changes to legal provision rather than an isolated tool; the supplied page does not specify regulatory mechanisms, adoption rates or economic effects.
qs: Instead, he predicts a world of online courts, AI-based global legal businesses, disruptive legal technologies, liberalized markets, commoditization, alternative sourcing, simulated practice on the metaverse, and many new legal jobs.

kp.k: Technology should address inaccessible and unaffordable legal services
kp.d: The description presents the book as challenging the profession's presumed immunity from technological change and urging the next generation to improve or overhaul legal and court services. It identifies unaffordability and inaccessibility for both businesses and citizens, without providing measurements of unmet need or demonstrated technological remedies.
qs: it challenges those who feel that the law and lawyers are somehow immune from technological advance
it draws attention to the unaffordability and inaccessibility of legal service, for businesses and citizens alike
it invites the next generation of lawyers to harness the power of technology in improving and even overhauling the way in which legal and court service is currently provided.

kp.k: Lawyers should help build replacements for outmoded work
kp.d: The book's stated recommendation is that lawyers actively build new systems rather than merely accommodate change. The publisher describes this as creating opportunities to help clients and communities and as both a privilege and an obligation. This is a normative career and professional recommendation, not evidence of realized job creation or displacement.
qs: It enjoins its readers to become involved in building the systems that will replace outmoded forms of legal work.
It argues that it is both a privilege and an obligation for tomorrow's lawyers to embrace and bring about change.

kp.k: New careers raise questions about legal training
kp.d: Susskind's forecast includes new legal jobs and simulated practice on the metaverse. The contents explicitly address new employment, the purposes of training and replacement of the old training ground. The supplied material establishes these as topics, but does not explain particular new roles, training designs or effects on junior-lawyer staffing.
qs: simulated practice on the metaverse, and many new legal jobs

kp.k: Transformation spans providers, buyers, courts and legal education
kp.d: The publisher characterizes the book's scope as the entire legal ecosystem, including law firms, in-house lawyers, alternative legal suppliers, technologists, startups, courts and educators. Online courts and online dispute resolution receive explicit coverage. The page does not supply separate findings about the effects on each group.
qs: Ranges across the entire legal ecosystem - covering law firms, in-house lawyers, alternative legal suppliers, judges and courts, legal education and educators, legal technologists, startups, and access to justice
Online Courts and Online Dispute Resolution

kp.k: Third edition adds pandemic, innovation and startup coverage
kp.d: The listing identifies new chapters on COVID-19's impact, innovation, lawtech startups and a model for understanding legal technology. These indicate the edition's expanded analytical scope; the supplied description does not state the model's components or the pandemic's specific effects.
qs: Includes new chapters on the impact of COVID-19, innovation in law, lawtech startups, and a model of understanding legal technology

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Susskind predicts AI-based global legal businesses and a broader transformation of legal delivery, markets and careers.
pts.d: The supplied document is OUP's publisher page, rather than the book itself. Its description attributes to Richard Susskind a future involving AI-based global legal businesses, online courts, disruptive technologies, liberalized markets, commoditization, alternative sourcing, metaverse-based simulated practice and new legal jobs. It also presents his call for lawyers to build systems that replace outmoded legal work. These are forecasts and recommendations, not reported empirical outcomes. The page does not specify which of the broader changes are caused specifically by AI, nor does it claim that all lawyers will be replaced.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The page grounds the forecasts in Susskind's professional experience and authority, without presenting empirical supporting evidence.
pts.d: OUP emphasizes 40 years of work in the field and describes Susskind's legal-technology advisory roles and doctoral research on AI and law. The supplied page offers no datasets, benchmarks, quantified adoption findings or case analyses supporting the forecasts. Its endorsements are praise for the author and book, not independent evidence of the predicted changes. This limitation concerns the supplied publisher page, not the contents of the full book.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The edition focuses on the 2020s and predicts exceptional change over the coming two decades.
pts.d: Published in March 2023, the page describes a focus on the 2020s and attributes to the book a prediction of more change over the coming two decades than over the previous two centuries, implying approximately 2023–2043. It gives no individual deadlines for AI-based businesses, online courts or new jobs, and no quantified definition of change. The description urges active participation by the next generation of lawyers in technological reform, but does not state formal conditions under which each forecast holds.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The envisaged changes span legal providers, corporate legal departments, courts, educators, aspiring lawyers and people needing legal help.
pts.d: Law firms and other legal providers face changes in service delivery and market organization; aspiring and young lawyers are offered a prospect of new jobs and participation in building replacement systems. In-house lawyers, courts, legal educators, technologists and startups are explicitly within the book's scope, although the page does not detail separate impacts for each. Businesses and citizens are identified as experiencing unaffordable and inaccessible services, which the call for technological reform seeks to address. This is not a measured claim that AI has reduced either enterprise legal costs or the public justice gap.
